title: Number of Good Pairs
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair of indices directly versus a running count per value, accumulated in one pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of integers nums, return the number of "good pairs," where a good pair is an index pair (i, j) with i strictly less than j and nums[i] equal to nums[j].

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, an integer array"],["Output","The count of index pairs with equal values"],["Goal","Count without checking every pair of indices directly"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 100; 1 <= nums[i] <= 100"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Pairs are only formed BETWEEN equal values","Group by value, then count pairs within each group"],["A value seen c times contributes exactly c choose 2 pairs","A running count per value, updated incrementally as each occurrence is encountered"]]}

blocks.text: Count how many pairs of index positions hold the exact same value, considering (i, j) and (j, i) as the same pair (only counted once, with i less than j).

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Handshakes Among People Wearing the Same Colored Shirt
blocks.text: Picture a group of people, some wearing matching colored shirts, and counting every possible handshake between two people wearing the SAME color. For a color worn by c people, the number of such handshakes is exactly c choose 2.

blocks.caption: A value seen c times so far contributes c new pairs when one more occurrence appears

blocks.text: The value 1 appears 3 times (3 choose 2 = 3 pairs), and the value 3 appears twice (1 pair), giving a total of 4.

Before checking every pair of indices directly, notice that pairs only ever form between equal values, so counting occurrences of each value directly gives the answer via a simple combinatorial formula.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A good pair requires nums[i] to equal nums[j], so only pairs of indices sharing the same value ever count.

Observation 2: If a value appears c times in total, the number of pairs among those c occurrences is exactly c choose 2, c times (c minus 1) divided by 2.

Observation 3: Rather than computing c choose 2 after counting every occurrence, the SAME total can be built incrementally: each time a value is seen again, it forms a new pair with every occurrence already seen, adding exactly that many pairs.

Observation 4: Tracking a running count per value in a hashmap, and adding the current count (before incrementing) to the answer at each occurrence, produces the correct total in one pass.
This leads to scanning nums once, maintaining a hashmap of value to occurrence count so far, and adding the current count to the answer before incrementing it, for every element.
Check every pair of indices directly, counting those with equal values.

items: For every pair of indices i less than j, check whether nums[i] equals nums[j].

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every pair of indices is compared directly, regardless of value.
This repeats the same comparison work for every value, even though only same-valued pairs ever matter.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), every pair of indices examined.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: comparing every pair directly ignores the fact that only same-valued pairs matter; counting occurrences of each value directly gives the answer with a single pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why pairwise comparison is wasteful: the answer only depends on how many times each distinct value occurs, not on comparing every individual pair of positions.

What formula replaces it: for a value occurring c times, it contributes c choose 2 pairs; summing this over every distinct value gives the total.

How to compute this in one pass: track a running count per value in a hashmap; each time a value is seen, add its CURRENT count (before this occurrence) to the answer, then increment its count.

The core idea: one pass, a hashmap of running counts, adding the current count to the answer at each occurrence.
Maintain a hashmap from value to how many times it has been seen so far. For each element in nums, add its current count in the hashmap to the running answer, then increment that count by 1.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: running count per value, add the current count before incrementing

blocks.text: Each time a value is seen, it forms a new pair with every occurrence of that same value already counted, exactly the running count stored in the hashmap. Summing this contribution at every occurrence exactly reproduces the total c choose 2 pairs for every distinct value, without ever computing that formula directly or comparing individual index pairs.

blocks.text: Number of Good Pairs is a clean example of turning a pairwise counting problem into a per-value running-count accumulation, avoiding both the pairwise comparison and the need to compute a combinatorial formula after the fact.

items: Counting occurrences first, then applying the c choose 2 formula in a second pass, instead of accumulating directly in one pass (both work, but the running-count version is simpler to get right).
Forgetting to increment the count AFTER adding it to the result, which would double count or miscount pairs.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["All elements distinct","The count is 0, no pairs exist."],["All elements identical","The count is n choose 2, the maximum possible."]]}

blocks.text: Explaining the running-count accumulation as equivalent to summing c choose 2 across values shows the underlying combinatorics clearly, even though the code itself never computes that formula explicitly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every pair", think: track a running count per value, adding it to the answer at each new occurrence.

items: How would you count pairs satisfying nums[i] equals nums[j] AND i times j is divisible by some k?
How would this generalize to counting triples with all three values equal?
Any "count pairs sharing a property" problem, solvable by grouping and applying (or accumulating) a combinatorial count per group.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized running-count approach runs in O(n) time. Space is O(1) for the brute force and O(distinct values) for the optimized approach.

items: Pattern: a running count per value, accumulating pairs incrementally as each occurrence is seen.
Core Idea: each new occurrence of a value pairs with every earlier occurrence already counted; adding the current count to the answer before incrementing captures this directly.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(distinct values) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: pairs only ever form between equal values, so grouping by value replaces pairwise comparison entirely.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, quick counting problem once the per-value accumulation is recognized.
One line memory trick: running count per value, add before incrementing.
